drills.q: p99 latency on a service is terrible but its CPU utilization dashboard shows comfortable headroom the entire time. What's your first hypothesis and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: CFS quota throttling within individual 100ms periods, invisible to a smoothed average. Confirm via container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total in Prometheus/cAdvisor; if the ratio is high, raise or remove the CPU limit for that workload.

drills.q: A Deployment has both HPA and VPA configured, both watching CPU. Replica count and per-pod sizing are both drifting unpredictably under steady load. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Classic HPA/VPA same-metric oscillation: VPA changes CPU requests, which changes HPA's utilization denominator, which changes replica count, which changes VPA's observed usage. Fix by splitting responsibility — VPA in updateMode: Off (recommend-only) or sizing memory instead, HPA driving off an independent metric like requests-per-second.

drills.q: Pods are stuck Pending, and neither Cluster Autoscaler nor Karpenter is provisioning new nodes even though the cluster is clearly out of capacity. What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether the pending pods have resources.requests set. Both tools decide to scale up based on determining a pod is unschedulable due to insufficient resources — pods with zero requests give no such signal and are invisible to the scale-up decision, so they sit Pending indefinitely.

drills.q: A traffic spike causes a multi-minute outage before new capacity comes online, even though autoscaling is configured correctly. What's the likely root cause and the fix?
drills.a: Cluster Autoscaler against node groups typically takes 4-8 minutes to bring a new node Ready, too slow for a spike-shaped traffic pattern. Migrate to Karpenter (~45-60s) for faster response, or maintain deliberate warm/buffer capacity for paths that can't tolerate multi-minute cold starts.

drills.q: A team wants to scale a Kafka consumer worker to zero replicas when the topic is empty, to save cost. Plain HPA can't do this. Why not, and what's the fix?
drills.a: HPA's algorithm computes desiredReplicas as a ratio against currentReplicas, requiring at least one running replica to have a metric to compute against — it structurally cannot decide to go from 0 to 1. KEDA adds a separate polling mechanism that watches the external event source (Kafka consumer lag) directly while the Deployment sits at zero, then hands off to a standard HPA it manages once replicas are above zero.

drills.q: Two GPU-inference pods land on the same GPU node, and one fails with an out-of-GPU-memory error even though the node's total GPU count looked sufficient. What happened?
drills.a: GPUs aren't fractionally shared by default — a pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 gets a whole physical GPU via the device plugin framework, and simply co-scheduling two pods doesn't make them safely share one device's memory. Real sharing needs an explicit mechanism: MIG (hardware-isolated partitions) or time-slicing (software, no isolation, real contention risk).

drills.q: A GPU workload's pod is stuck Pending and kubectl describe node shows the target GPU node has free GPU capacity. What's the most likely single cause?
drills.a: The pod is missing the toleration for the GPU node pool's taint (commonly nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule). GPU nodes are near-universally tainted to keep ordinary CPU-only workloads off them, and a pod without the matching toleration is excluded from scheduling there regardless of free capacity.

drills.q: A latency-sensitive service is set to Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for both CPU and memory) to protect it from eviction. What tradeoff did this choice quietly introduce?
drills.a: Guaranteed QoS requires a CPU limit equal to the request, which reintroduces CFS-quota throttling risk for exactly the workload where tail latency matters most — there's a real tension between eviction protection (favors Guaranteed) and avoiding throttling (favors no CPU limit, at best Burstable), and the right choice depends on which failure mode is worse for that specific service.
